To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hydrophobically hydrated Pr4N(++) is stabilized on the CO-covered Pt surface, and its water shell is destroyed by applying an electrochemical force to approach the CO-covered Pt.
the hydrophobically hydrated Pr4N(+(aq)) cations are initially attracted to the hydrophobic Pt surface and are stabilized there.
the destruction of the hydration shells of hydrated cations is a dynamic process that can be directly observed in real time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the direct observation of major alterations or destruction of hydration shells around hydrated ions or molecules under electrochemical force in real time.

the direct real-time observation of the alteration of the hydration shell of a solute molecule or ion under electrochemical force, and provides new information on the structure and stability of hydration shells.
the direct observation of the destruction and reconstruction of the hydration shell of solutes in solution under electrochemical force.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the destruction of the hydration shells is a rather slow process, taking a few hundreds of milliseconds.
the hydrophobically stabilized hydration shell is destroyed by the application of a strong enough force, but this process is slow, taking a long time to complete.

the hydrophobically stabilized hydration shell of Pr(4)(+) is destroyed by the strong electrostatic interaction with the hydrophobic CO surface, while the Na(+) hydration shell is not destroyed by the hydrophilic surface, even when the force between them is strong.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the hydration shell of solutes in solution is not a passive spectator in solution, but is rather a dynamic structure that is involved in the interaction between solutes and surfaces, and the hydration structure can be altered or destroyed by external forces.
hydrophobic interactions between solutes and hydrophobic surfaces are stronger than the interactions between solutes themselves, which is consistent with the hydrophobic effect.
the hydration shells around ions or molecules in close contact with a surface can be destroyed by applying an electrochemical force, and that the destruction is slower for hydrophobic solutes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
electrostatic forces are not sufficient to destroy the hydration shell of a hydrated cation approaching a hydrophobic surface.
the hydration shell of Pr(4+) is not only strongly bound to the solute but also to the surface, whereas Na(+) is only strongly bound to its hydration shell and not to the surface.
hydration shells around interacting solutes can be directly observed by using an IR absorption spectroscopic technique.
